gloss: die; kill, put to death; death; the dead
summary: מוּת is to die: to come to the end of life, said alike of man, beast, fish and tree, by old age, sickness, sword, famine or the sentence of a judge. Its causative is to kill or put to death, and its participle מֵת is the dead man, the corpse. The noun מָוֶת is death, the opposite of life (Deu 30:19): the end to which all the living come, the sentence on sin (Gen 2:17; Ezk 18:4), a deadly plague, and, set beside Sheol, the silent state of the dead where there is no remembrance or praise of Yahweh (Psa 6:6). Scripture calls it a sleep from which the dead are to be woken (Psa 13:4; Dan 12:2), and promises that Yahweh will swallow it up for ever (Isa 25:8). Every Semitic language has the root with the same meaning.

words.gloss: die; (hiphil, polel) kill, put to death; (participle) dead, a dead man
words.summary: About 830 times: some 620 in the qal, 137 in the hiphil, 68 in the hophal and 9 in the polel. The count under its key is higher by 36 tokens spelled מוֹת that are the construct of the noun מָוֶת (“the death of”), and the noun's count holds 50 of the verb's infinitive absolutes (מוֹת תָּמוּת). The perfect and the participle are both מֵת, so “he died”, “he is dead” and “a dead man” are one word.

stems.gloss: die; die for an offence; be dead, a dead man, the dead

senses.gloss: die, come to the end of life
senses.definition: To cease to live: the end of a man's days, whether in old age, by sickness, in childbirth, by the sword, famine or plague, or at Yahweh's hand. It is the opposite of living, it is followed by burial, and it comes to every man.

evidence.note: “All the days of Adam that he lived were 930 years, וַיָּמֹת”: dying is the end of the days a man lives; the refrain of the chapter.
“Abraham expired and died (וַיִּגְוַע וַיָּמָת) in a good old age, old and full, and was gathered to his people.”
“That we may live and not die (וְנִחְיֶה וְלֹא נָמוּת)”: the opposite of living. So Deu 33:6; Psa 118:17; 2Ki 20:1.
“Man dies and is laid low; man expires, and where is he?”
“The living know שֶׁיָּמֻתוּ, that they will die.”
“The wise die; the fool and the brute alike perish, and leave their wealth to others.”
“For we shall surely die, and are like water spilled on the ground, which is not gathered up.”
“A time to be born and a time to die.”
“Gideon died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father.”
“Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, at the mouth of Yahweh.”
Rachel in childbirth: “as her soul was going out, for she was dying (כִּי מֵתָה)”.
In battle: “many of the people have fallen and died, and Saul and Jonathan his son are dead.”
“The young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine.”
The spies “died by the plague before Yahweh”.
“Let my soul die (תָּמֹת נַפְשִׁי) the death of the upright”: it is the soul that dies. So Jdg 16:30; Job 36:14.
“If a man dies, shall he live? All the days of my service I will wait, till my change comes.”
“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die”; quoted in 1Co 15:32 as what follows if the dead are not raised.

senses.gloss: die (of beasts, fish, plants); fail, come to an end
senses.definition: The same verb for every creature in which is the breath of life, for a tree's stock in the ground, and by figure for a heart that fails, a land left desolate and a nation brought to its end.

evidence.note: “All in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, of all that was on the dry land, died”: man and beast together in the flood.
“The fish that were in the river died.”
“All the livestock of Egypt died.”
“If any beast which is yours for food dies.”
Of a felled tree: “its stock dies in the dust”.
Of the carcasses of the rebels: “their worm shall not die”; quoted in Mrk 9:48.
Nabal: “his heart died within him and he became a stone”; he himself died about ten days later (v. 38). The heart's dying is its failing.
“Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land?”
“Moab shall die in tumult.”
“With you wisdom will die.”

senses.gloss: die for an offence, be put to death
senses.definition: To die as the penalty of sin or crime, by the sentence of God or of a judge. The infinitive before the verb, מוֹת תָּמוּת, makes the sentence certain.

evidence.note: “In the day you eat of it מוֹת תָּמוּת, you shall surely die.”
“The soul that sins, it shall die (הִיא תָמוּת).” So v. 20.
The man who will not hear the priest or the judge: “that man shall die, and you shall put away the evil from Israel.”
Solomon to Shimei: “in the day you go out … know for certain that you shall surely die; your blood shall be on your own head.” He was put to death after he had gone and returned (vv. 42, 46).
To Abimelech: “if you do not restore her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours.”
Saul: “you shall surely die, Jonathan”; the people ransomed him “and he did not die” (v. 45).
Nadab and Abihu: fire went out from Yahweh and consumed them, “and they died before Yahweh”.
Of the priest's service done as commanded: “that he may not die”. So Exo 30:20; Lev 16:2; Num 4:20.
“He died in his own sin.”
“Every one shall die in his own iniquity.”
“When I say to the wicked, You shall surely die … he shall die in his iniquity.”
“At the mouth of two witnesses or three shall he who is to die be put to death”; cited in Heb 10:28.

senses.gloss: be dead; a dead person, a corpse; the dead
senses.definition: The participle מֵת: one who has died. As a noun it is the dead person to be buried, the corpse that makes unclean, and in the plural the dead as a class, set against the living. It is also said of a living man who is under sentence of death or as good as dead.

evidence.note: Abraham of Sarah: “that I may bury my dead (מֵתִי) out of my sight.”
“The living know that they will die, but הַמֵּתִים, the dead, know nothing.”
“The dead do not praise Yah, nor any who go down to silence.”
“He who touches the dead (בְּמֵת), any soul of man, shall be unclean seven days.”
The Nazirite “shall not come near נֶפֶשׁ מֵת, a dead soul”. So Lev 21:11.
“There was not a house where there was not one dead.”
Yahweh's kindness “to the living and to the dead”.
“A living dog is better than the dead lion.”
Forbidden in Israel: “one who seeks to the dead (דֹרֵשׁ אֶל־הַמֵּתִים)”.
“Should not a people seek to its God? To the dead on behalf of the living?”
“Will you do a wonder for the dead? Will the Rephaim rise and thank you?”
“I am forgotten like a dead man, out of mind.”
Of the lords who had ruled Israel: “dead, they shall not live.”
“Your dead shall live (יִחְיוּ מֵתֶיךָ); my corpses shall rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust.”
Elisha “had made the dead live”.
God to the living Abimelech: “הִנְּךָ מֵת, behold, you are a dead man, because of the woman you have taken”: dead as under sentence of death (v. 7).
Rachel: “give me children, or else I am dead (מֵתָה אָנֹכִי).”
David of himself: “after a dead dog”.

senses.definition: To cause to die. Men kill in murder, in war and in carrying out a sentence; Yahweh kills and makes alive; a lion or an ox kills; and a man's own envy or desire kills him.

evidence.note: “I kill and I make alive (אֲנִי אָמִית וַאֲחַיֶּה); I wound and I heal.”
“Yahweh kills and makes alive (מֵמִית וּמְחַיֶּה); he brings down to the grave and brings up.”
“Am I God, to kill and to make alive?”
Er “was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and Yahweh killed him”.
“Far be it from you … to kill the righteous with the wicked.”
Joseph's brothers “conspired against him to kill him”.
Saul spoke to his servants “to kill David”.
Joshua took their kings, “struck them and killed them”.
In carrying out a sentence: “the hand of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death.”
“The redeemer of blood, he shall put the manslayer to death.”
“A lion met him on the way and killed him.”
The ox that “kills a man or a woman”.
“Jealousy kills the simple.”
“The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to work.”
Of the shoot from Jesse: “with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.”
Jeremiah: “if you put me to death, you bring innocent blood on yourselves.”

senses.definition: To be killed by sentence: the law's word for the penalty of a capital offence, usually as מוֹת יוּמָת, “he shall surely be put to death”.

evidence.note: “He who strikes a man so that he dies (וָמֵת), מוֹת יוּמָת”: the qal for the victim's death, the hophal for the killer's.
“Fathers shall not be put to death for sons, nor sons for fathers; each shall be put to death for his own sin.” Kept by Amaziah, 2Ki 14:6.
“He who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death”; quoted by Jesus as God's commandment, Mat 15:4; Mrk 7:10.
The blasphemer of the name of Yahweh: “all the congregation shall stone him.”
“You shall take no ransom for the life of a manslayer who is guilty of death, for he shall surely be put to death.”
“If there is in a man a sin worthy of death and he is put to death (וְהוּמָת), and you hang him on a tree.”
The profaner of the sabbath.
“The stranger who comes near shall be put to death.”
Abimelech's decree: “whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.”
David: “shall a man be put to death in Israel today?”
Athaliah “was put to death there”.

senses.definition: To make an end of one by killing him, most often one already struck down or dying; in the Psalms, to hound to death.

evidence.note: Abimelech, his skull crushed by a millstone: “draw your sword וּמוֹתְתֵנִי, and kill me, lest they say, A woman killed him.”
Saul, fallen on the field: “stand over me and kill me, for agony has seized me”; v. 10, “I killed him, for I knew that he could not live after he had fallen.”
David, the Philistine already felled by the stone, “drew his sword and killed him (וַיְמֹתְתֵהוּ) and cut off his head”.
They fell before Jonathan, “and his armour-bearer was killing after him”.
“Because he did not kill me from the womb.”
“Evil shall kill the wicked.”
He pursued the poor and the broken in heart “to kill him”.

evidence.locator: Gen.2.17, תָּמוּת → ἀποθανεῖσθε; Isa.22.13, נָמוּת → ἀποθνῄσκομεν; Deu.25.5, מֵת → ἀποθάνῃ; Deu.17.6, יוּמַת → ἀποθανεῖται; Ezk.18.4 → ἀποθανεῖται; ἀποθνήσκω renders מוּת ×374

evidence.note: Isa 22:13 quoted: “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (ἀποθνῄσκομεν).”
Deu 25:5 cited: “if a man dies (ἀποθάνῃ) having no children.”
Deu 17:6: he who set aside Moses' law “dies without mercy on two or three witnesses”.
“As in Adam all die, so in the Christ shall all be made alive.”
“Lazarus has died (ἀπέθανεν).”

evidence.locator: Exo.21.17, יוּמָת → τελευτήσει; Isa.66.24, תָמוּת → τελευτήσει; τελευτάω renders מוּת ×23

evidence.note: Exo 21:17 quoted: “let him die the death (θανάτῳ τελευτάτω)”, the Hebrew מוֹת יוּמָת; so Mrk 7:10.
Isa 66:24 quoted: “where their worm does not die (οὐ τελευτᾷ).”
Of David: “he both died (ἐτελεύτησεν) and was buried.”

evidence.locator: 1Sa.17.51, וַיְמֹתְתֵהוּ → ἐθανάτωσεν; Exo.21.12, יוּמָת → θανατούσθω; 1Sa.2.6, מֵמִית → θανατοῖ; θανατόω renders מוּת ×45

evidence.note: The council sought false witness against Jesus “that they might put him to death (θανατώσωσιν)”.
“Children will rise up against parents and put them to death.”
Christ “put to death (θανατωθείς) in flesh, but made alive in spirit”.
“If by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.”

evidence.locator: Psa.115.17, הַמֵּתִים → νεκροί; Ecc.9.5, הַמֵּתִים → νεκροί; νεκρός renders the participle מֵת ×16

evidence.note: “He is not a God of the dead (νεκρῶν) but of the living”: said to show that the dead are raised (v. 37).
“I became dead (νεκρός), and behold, I am living for the ages of the ages.”
“The dead shall be raised incorruptible.”

parallels.note: “Expire, breathe one's last”: joined with מוּת of the patriarchs' deaths, and set beside it in Job.
“Lie down”: to die is to lie down with one's fathers, and not to rise until woken.

evidence.note: “You are about to lie down with your fathers”, said when Moses' “days draw near to die” (v. 14).
After “man dies” (v. 10): “man lies down and does not rise … they shall not be roused from their sleep.”

parallels.note: “Perish”: the wise die and the fool perishes alike.

evidence.note: “When will he die, and his name perish?”

parallels.note: “Fall”: of death in battle and of the fall of the great.

evidence.note: “You shall die like man, and fall like one of the princes.”

opposites.note: “Live”: to live and not die; the hiphil's opposite is “make alive”.

evidence.note: “I shall not die, but live.”
“He shall surely live; he shall not die.”
“You are dying and shall not live.”
“I kill and I make alive.”

phrases.gloss: you shall surely die (“dying you shall die”): the sentence made certain

evidence.note: The serpent's denial: “לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן, you shall not surely die.”

phrases.gloss: he shall surely be put to death: the law's capital sentence
and he died and was buried
he was sick to the point of dying
one who seeks to the dead (forbidden)

evidence.note: The final words follow “he will guide us”. Read as a preposition and infinitive, they may mark the limit of that guidance. The wording has also been read as a musical direction.

words.gloss: death; the state of the dead; a deadly plague
words.summary: About 160 times (construct מוֹת; with the old ending הַמָּוְתָה, Psa 116:15; plural “deaths” in Ezk 28:10 and Isa 53:9). The count under its key is higher by 50 infinitive absolutes of the verb. The compound צַלְמָוֶת, “shadow of death”, is filed with צֵל and is not counted here.

senses.definition: The event of dying and the fact of being dead: the opposite of life, the end that comes to every man and beast and from which no man delivers himself.

evidence.note: “Life and death (הַחַיִּים וְהַמָּוֶת) I have set before you, the blessing and the curse; choose life, that you may live.” So v. 15; Jer 21:8.
“What man shall live and not see death, shall deliver his soul from the hand of the grave?”
Of man and beast: “as the death of the one, so the death of the other, and all have one breath.”
“If these die as all men die (כְּמוֹת כָּל־הָאָדָם)”: death is common to all.
“I do not know the day of my death.”
“After the death of Moses”: the usual mark of time. So Jdg 1:1; 2Sa 1:1; Num 35:25.
“There is but a step between me and death.”
“If anything but death parts you and me.”
“Whether for death or for life, there will your servant be.”
“No man has power over the day of death.”
“Death and life are in the hand of the tongue.”
“Let my soul die the death of the upright.”
“Precious in the eyes of Yahweh is the death (הַמָּוְתָה) of his faithful ones.”
The servant “poured out his soul to death”.
“I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies.” So v. 23; 33:11.
The plural, a manner of dying: “you shall die the deaths of the uncircumcised.”

senses.gloss: death as the state and place of the dead
senses.definition: Death as where the dead are: set beside Sheol (the grave), Abaddon and the pit, with gates, cords and chambers, a place of dust, silence and forgetting, where Yahweh is not remembered or praised. Spoken of as a power that shepherds, devours and is never satisfied, and that Yahweh will swallow up.

evidence.note: “In death there is no remembrance of you; in the grave who will give you thanks?”
“The grave does not thank you, death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your truth.”
“From the hand of the grave I will ransom them; from death I will redeem them”; quoted in 1Co 15:55.
“He will swallow up death for ever (בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח)”; quoted in 1Co 15:54.
“Like sheep they are appointed for the grave; death shall shepherd them.”
“Abaddon and death say, We have heard a report of it.”
“Have the gates of death been opened to you?”
“You will bring me to death, the house appointed for all the living.”
“You lay me in the dust of death.”
“The cords of death encompassed me … the cords of the grave surrounded me; the snares of death confronted me.”
“Her house is the way to the grave, going down to the chambers of death.” So Pro 5:5.
“We have made a covenant with death, and with the grave we have an agreement”; v. 18, it shall not stand.
The proud man “enlarges his desire like the grave, and is like death, and is not satisfied”.
“Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as the grave.”
“Lest I sleep the death (פֶּן־אִישַׁן הַמָּוֶת)”: death as a sleep.

senses.definition: Death as the penalty a man is liable to: a “judgment of death”, a “sin of death”, and the man under it a “son of death” or “man of death”.

evidence.note: “If there is in a man חֵטְא מִשְׁפַּט־מָוֶת, a sin with a judgment of death, and he is put to death.”
The priests of Jeremiah: “a judgment of death for this man!”; the princes, v. 16: “there is no judgment of death for this man.”
The unwitting manslayer “had no judgment of death”.
“There is in the girl no sin of death.”
Saul of David: “he is a son of death (בֶן־מָוֶת)”.
David of the rich man in Nathan's parable: “the man who has done this is a son of death.”
Solomon to Abiathar: “you are a man of death (אִישׁ מָוֶת), but I will not put you to death today.”

senses.gloss: deadly plague, pestilence; a deadly thing
senses.definition: Death by disease, named beside the sword, famine and captivity as one of Yahweh's judgments; and anything that brings death, as a plague of locusts or poison in a pot.

evidence.note: “Those for death, to death; those for the sword, to the sword; those for famine, to famine; those for captivity, to captivity”: death here is one judgment among four, where Ezk 14:21 has דֶּבֶר, pestilence. So Jer 43:11.
“Let their men be slain by death, their young men struck by the sword in battle.”
“Those who survive him shall be buried by death.”
Pharaoh of the locusts: “that he may take away from me only this death (הַמָּוֶת הַזֶּה).”
“There is death in the pot, man of God!”
Of the healed waters: “there shall be from there no more death or miscarrying.”
“Death has come up into our windows; it has entered our palaces.”
The Greek and the Peshitta use “death” in the same way: power “to kill with sword, with famine, with death (ἐν θανάτῳ, בְּמַותָּא) and by the beasts of the earth”, the four judgments of Ezk 14:21.

evidence.locator: Isa.25.8, הַמָּוֶת → ὁ θάνατος; Hos.13.14, מָוֶת → θάνατε; Deu.30.19 → θάνατον; Psa.18.5 → θανάτου; Jer.15.2 → θάνατον; θάνατος renders מָוֶת ×76 (and the infinitive absolute מוֹת as θανάτῳ, Gen.2.17; Exo.21.12); it also renders דֶּבֶר “pestilence”, Ezk.14.21; Jer.14.12

evidence.note: Isa 25:8 quoted: “death (ὁ θάνατος) is swallowed up in victory.”
Hos 13:14 quoted: “where, death, is your sting? Where, grave, is your victory?”
Exo 21:17: θανάτῳ τελευτάτω for מוֹת יוּמָת.
“Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin.”
“The wages of sin is death.”
“The last enemy to be abolished is death.”
“Having loosed the pangs of death (τὰς ὠδῖνας τοῦ θανάτου)”: the Septuagint's words for חֶבְלֵי־מָוֶת, Psa 18:5; 116:3.
θάνατος as pestilence, with sword, famine and beasts; so Rev 2:23.

parallels.note: Sheol, the grave: the constant pair of מָוֶת in poetry.
“Shadow of death”, deep darkness: its gates beside the gates of death.
“Evil”: death and evil against life and good.

opposites.note: “Life”: the two are set before Israel to choose between.

evidence.note: “The way of life and the way of death.”
“A fountain of life, to turn from the snares of death.”
“My death is better than my life.”

phrases.gloss: a son of death: one who deserves to die
a man of death: one liable to death
a judgment of death: a capital sentence
no death: in the path of righteousness

evidence.note: “In the path of righteousness is life, and in the way of its track אַל־מָוֶת, no death.”

words.summary: Twice only, both in the plural construct מְמוֹתֵי with the verb, of the kind of death men die: scripture fixes it no further than those two verses. Arabic has the same formation, مَمَات.

senses.definition: The death one dies, named by its cause: deaths of diseases, the deaths of the slain.

evidence.note: “מְמוֹתֵי תַחֲלֻאִים יָמֻתוּ, they shall die deaths of diseases; they shall not be lamented or buried.”
To the prince of Tyre: “you shall die the deaths of the slain (מְמוֹתֵי חָלָל) in the heart of the seas.”

words.gloss: death (in “sons of death”, those doomed to die)
words.summary: Twice only, both in the phrase בְּנֵי תְמוּתָה, “sons of death”, beside the groaning of the prisoner: scripture fixes it no further. The phrase is formed as בֶּן־מָוֶת is.

senses.definition: In “sons of death”: prisoners appointed to die, whom Yahweh is asked to preserve and looses.

evidence.note: “Let the groaning of the prisoner come before you; according to the greatness of your arm preserve בְּנֵי תְמוּתָה.”
Yahweh looks from heaven “to hear the groaning of the prisoner, to loose the sons of death”.

words.summary: Scripture's Aramaic has the noun once, in Artaxerxes' letter, as the first of the penalties of the law; Daniel and Ezra use קְטַל for killing and have no verb of this root.

senses.definition: Death as the heaviest sentence of a court.

evidence.note: “Let judgment be done on him with diligence, whether for death (הֵן לְמוֹת), or banishment, or confiscation of goods, or bonds.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's verb for dying, about 170 times, where the Greek has ἀποθνήσκω, τελευτάω and θνήσκω; its imperfect is נְמוּת, with the ו of the Hebrew, and its infinitive before the verb (מְמָת נְמוּת) answers to מוֹת יוּמָת.

senses.definition: To come to the end of life; said of Lazarus, of David, of all men in Adam, and of Christ.

evidence.note: After “Lazarus has fallen asleep”: “then Jesus said to them plainly, לָעָזַר מִית, Lazarus has died.”
“As in Adam all men die (מָיתִּין), so in the Messiah all live.”
Exo 21:17 in Jesus' mouth: “he who reviles his father or his mother מְמָת נְמוּת, shall surely die”: the Hebrew idiom kept.
Deu 25:5: “if a man dies having no sons.”
Of David: “he died (דְּמִית) and also was buried.”
“The Messiah died for our sins, as it is written.”
“It is appointed to men that they die once, and after their death the judgment.”
Isa 66:24: “their worm does not die (לָא מָיתָּא).”
“He who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live.”

senses.definition: By figure: to be done with a thing as the dead are done with life.

evidence.note: “In that he died, he died to sin once.”
“You also have died to the law through the body of the Messiah.”

senses.definition: To cause to die, as the Hebrew hiphil; also of putting to death the deeds of the body.

evidence.note: The council sought witnesses against Jesus “that they might put him to death (דַּנְמִיתוּנָיהִי)”. So Mat 27:1; Mrk 14:55.
“Children shall rise against their parents and put them to death.”
“If by the spirit you put to death (מְמִיתִין) the practices of the body, you live.”
“Put to death (אַמִיתוּ) therefore your members which are on the earth.”

senses.definition: The end of life, which came in by sin and reigns over all men; set with Sheol as the Hebrew is, and to be brought to nothing.

evidence.note: “By one man sin entered the world, and by sin death (מַותָּא), and so death passed on all the sons of men, because they all sinned.”
Isa 25:8 and Hos 13:14: “death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your sting, death? Where is your victory, Sheol?”: the Peshitta keeps Hosea's pair, death and Sheol.
“The last enemy, death, is brought to nothing.”
“The wages of sin is death.”

doctrine.statement: Yahweh God said to the man, “in the day you eat of it you shall surely die (מוֹת תָּמוּת)” (Gen 2:17); the serpent said to the woman, “you shall not surely die” (Gen 3:4). When they had eaten, the sentence Yahweh passed on the man was this: “until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Gen 3:19); and he sent him out of the garden “lest he put out his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever” (Gen 3:22). Adam lived 930 years, “and he died” (Gen 5:5). The same form of words is spoken to Shimei, “in the day you go out and cross the wadi Kidron, know for certain that you shall surely die” (1Ki 2:37), and he was put to death after he had gone to Gath and come back (1Ki 2:42, 46); and God says to Abimelech while he lives, “behold, you are a dead man (הִנְּךָ מֵת) because of the woman”, and, “if you do not restore her, know that you shall surely die” (Gen 20:3, 7). Paul writes that “through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed to all men, because all sinned” (Rom 5:12), that “through a man came death” and “in Adam all die” (1Co 15:21–22), and that “the wages of sin is death” (Rom 6:23); James, that sin when it is finished brings forth death (Jas 1:15). From the verses: death came into the world by sin and is its wages. What the death is, the sentence itself says: the return of the man to the dust he was made from. In the day he ate, the man came under that sentence and was shut out from living for ever, as Shimei and Abimelech were dead men from the day of their offence; and the word that failed was the serpent's, that the sinner would not die.

When a man dies, “his breath goes out, he returns to his ground; in that very day his thoughts perish” (Psa 146:4); of all creatures, “you take away their breath, they expire and return to their dust” (Psa 104:29). “The living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing … their love and their hatred and their envy have already perished” (Ecc 9:5–6), and “there is no work or reckoning or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, the grave, where you are going” (Ecc 9:10). “In death there is no remembrance of you; in the grave who will give you thanks?” (Psa 6:6); “the dead do not praise Yah, nor any who go down to silence” (Psa 115:17); “the grave does not thank you, death does not praise you … the living, the living, he thanks you” (Isa 38:18–19). Man has no advantage over the beast in this: “as the one dies, so dies the other, and all have one breath … all are from the dust, and all return to the dust” (Ecc 3:19–20). It is the soul that dies: “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezk 18:4), Balaam and Samson say “let my soul die” (Num 23:10; Jdg 16:30), and a corpse is “a dead soul” (Num 6:6). Peter says of David that “he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day”, and that “David did not ascend into the heavens” (Act 2:29, 34). The law forbids seeking to the dead (Deu 18:11), and Isaiah asks, “should a people seek to the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isa 8:19). It is God “who alone has immortality” (1Ti 6:16). From the verses: death is the end of the whole man, his breath, his thought, his feeling and his praise of God; scripture speaks of no part of him that lives on through it; and the dead are in the grave, knowing nothing, until they are raised.

David prays, “lighten my eyes, lest I sleep the death” (Psa 13:4). When Moses' “days draw near to die”, Yahweh tells him, “you are about to lie down with your fathers” (Deu 31:14, 16), and “David lay down with his fathers and was buried” (1Ki 2:10). Job says, “man dies and is laid low … man lies down and does not rise; till the heavens are no more they shall not awake, nor be roused from their sleep” (Job 14:10, 12). Daniel is told that “many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground shall awake, some to life of the age, and some to reproaches” (Dan 12:2). Jesus says, “our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to wake him”; John explains that “Jesus had spoken of his death”, and Jesus then says plainly, “Lazarus has died” (Jhn 11:11–14). Stephen “fell asleep” (Act 7:60); David “fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption” (Act 13:36); Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep”, and if he was not raised, “those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (1Co 15:18, 20); and at the Lord's coming “the dead in Christ shall rise first” (1Th 4:13–16). From the verses: scripture's own figure for death is sleep, a state without knowledge from which the sleeper must be woken; the waking is the resurrection at the coming of Christ, and without it the dead would have perished.

Isaiah's servant “poured out his soul to death” and was given a grave (Isa 53:9, 12). Paul delivered first of all “that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised the third day” (1Co 15:3–4); he “became obedient as far as death” (Php 2:8). In the days of his flesh he prayed “to him who was able to save him out of death, and was heard” (Heb 5:7), and “God raised him up, having loosed the pangs of death” (Act 2:24), the cords of death and of the grave of Psa 18:5–6. He says of himself, “I became dead, and behold, I am living for the ages of the ages, and I have the keys of the grave and of death” (Rev 1:18); and Paul, that “Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom 6:9). God is the one “who alone has immortality” (1Ti 6:16). From the verses: Jesus died as men die and was dead until God raised him. One who died, and was saved out of death by another to whom he prayed, is a man, the son of the God who cannot die. Since he was raised, death has no more hold on him, and its keys are in his hand.

Isaiah says that Yahweh “will swallow up death for ever, and the Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from all faces” (Isa 25:8), and, “your dead shall live; my corpses shall rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust” (Isa 26:19). Through Hosea Yahweh says, “from the hand of the grave I will ransom them; from death I will redeem them” (Hos 13:14). Paul quotes Isaiah and Hosea of the day of the last trumpet, when “the dead shall be raised incorruptible” and “this mortal shall put on immortality”: “then shall come to pass the word that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, death, is your sting?” (1Co 15:51–55). “As in Adam all die, so in the Christ shall all be made alive”, each in his order, Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his coming; “the last enemy to be abolished is death” (1Co 15:22–23, 26). Christ “abolished death and brought life and incorruption to light through the gospel” (2Ti 1:10). John sees death and the grave cast into the lake of fire, and hears that “death shall be no more” (Rev 20:14; 21:4). From the verses: what scripture sets against death is the raising of the dead and the gift of immortality at Christ's coming, not a life that continues through death; and death itself is to come to an end.

Moses says to Israel, “I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse; choose life, that you may live” (Deu 30:15, 19), and Jeremiah, “behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death” (Jer 21:8). Ezekiel says that “the soul that sins, it shall die”, each for his own sin and not for his father's (Ezk 18:4, 20; Deu 24:16); yet “if the wicked turns from all his sins … he shall surely live; he shall not die”, for “I have no pleasure in the death of him who dies … turn, and live” (Ezk 18:21, 32; 33:11). Jesus says that he who hears his word and believes him who sent him “has passed out of death into life” (Jhn 5:24), and, “he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (Jhn 11:25). Paul says that those baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death and buried with him, to walk in newness of life and to share the likeness of his resurrection (Rom 6:3–5), and that “the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is life of the age in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom 6:23). From the verses: the two ends set before men are death and life, not two kinds of life; God does not wish the sinner's death; and the way out of it is in Christ, entered by belief and by baptism into his death.

note: Drafted 2026-11-15. ROOT: מות is the key the database files the words under (m.be.aa and following), and it is the root itself, so the brief's key is kept. COUNTS: the brief counts by spelling, so m.be.aa (870) includes 36 tokens of the noun's construct מוֹת (Gen 21:16; 25:11; Jos 1:1 and the rest), and m.be.ab (209) includes 50 infinitive absolutes מוֹת of the verb (Gen 2:17; Exo 21:12 and the rest); the summaries say so. Cross-reference keys with no tokens (m.ck.ai מְמוֹתִים, m.dz.ac מֵת, w.ax.af תְּמוּתָה) are left off. LEFT OUT: צַלְמָוֶת (r.cc.ae, filed under צלל) is a compound of צֵל and מָוֶת as pointed and belongs with צֵל's entry; it is named here only as a parallel (Job 38:17). The names אֲחִימוֹת (a.ck.an) and עַזְמָוֶת (p.bx.at) have name entries ahimoth and azmaveth; חֲצַרְמָוֶת already has hazarmaveth (under chatsotsrah). The place (בֵּית) עַזְמָוֶת (p.bx.au; Ezr 2:24; Neh 7:28; 12:29) is a place and has no entry. NOT ENTERED: the polal/hophal ketiv of 2Ki 11:2 (ממותתים, qere מוּמָתִים) is read with the qere under the hophal count. The final phrase עַל־מוּת in Psalm 48:15 is treated under usage. The similarly written heading of Psalm 9:1 is in mut-labben. Hab 1:12 לֹא נָמוּת (“we shall not die”, with an old scribal note that it stood “you do not die”) is not cited. Isa 53:9 בְּמֹתָיו is taken as the plural of מָוֶת (“in his deaths”), as Ezk 28:10 מוֹתֵי. Job 33:22 לַמְמִתִים (hiphil participle, “the slayers”) is not cited. SENSES: the “pestilence” sense of מָוֶת rests on Jer 15:2; 43:11; 18:21; Job 27:15 beside Ezk 14:21, on Sabaic mwt, Arabic مُوتَان and Aramaic מוֹתָנָא, and on the Septuagint's and Revelation's θάνατος for דֶּבֶר; a reviewer may prefer to fold it into “death”. PESHITTA: the brief found no Peshitta root because SEDRA keys it מת (root 1036): lexemes 1727 מות (verb, 171 NT tokens), 1728 מותא (125), 1732 מיתא (126), 1729 מותנא (2: Mat 24:7; Luk 21:11), 1730 מיותותא (2: 1Co 15:53, 54), 1733 מיתותא (2: 2Co 4:10; 5:4); lexeme 1731 מייתא (Heb 11:4, Abel “though dead”) is not entered as a word. The Syriac lemmas are written from SEDRA's vocalised forms; Payne Smith not consulted. The Peshitta at Act 2:24 has “the cords of Sheol” where the Greek has “the pangs of death”; at 1Ti 6:16 “who alone is incorruptible” where the Greek has “who alone has immortality” (the doctrine quotes the Greek); at Heb 2:14 it names the one having the power of death סָטָנָא where the Greek has τὸν διάβολον. DOCTRINE not written: Heb 2:14 (through death he brought to nothing the one having the power of death, the false accuser) and Rev 2:11; 20:6; 21:8 (the second death) bear on this root but need their own treatment (sin in the flesh; the judgment) and are left for review; Isa 65:20 (death still present in the age Isaiah describes) likewise. The reading of Gen 2:17 “in the day” follows the parallels in 1Ki 2:37 and Gen 20:3; review. COGNATES: Segert, Krahmalkov and Biella were read from the local text layers (OCR), pages taken from the printed running heads, PDFs not rendered; Segert's tmtt entry is printed “tmit” by the OCR. Ugaritic script forms are written from the transliteration. Ge'ez is cited from Wiktionary; Dillmann and Leslau not checked. Leads not followed: Egyptian mwt “die” (not Semitic, and TLA's lemma for the verb was not found in the vendored list: the brief's hits are mw.t “mother” and the goddess Mut); Old Aramaic and Deir ʿAlla attestations; DULAT for Ugaritic mt and the god Mot; CAD for mâtu, mūtu, mītu; the chess term (shah) mat. GREEK: θνήσκω (×43 for מוּת in the Septuagint) and ἀποκτείνω (×35) are not entered, having no New Testament quotation of a verse of this root found; no Greek loan from this root.
